messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Henry had been working as a cashier at a small grocery store for nearly 20 years when he finally decided to retire and move back to his hometown. He had grown up in Eastern Europe, where his family had lived through the devastating effects of war. As a young man, Henry had witnessed the horrors of combat firsthand, watching as his neighborhood was bombed and his friends were killed. The memories of that time had always lingered, but it wasn't until he lost his wife to illness five years ago that they began to overwhelm him. He found himself constantly on edge, unable to shake the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. Simple tasks like driving or riding in a car became unbearable, as he would scan the road for potential threats and flinch at every sudden noise. Henry tried to distract himself by replaying the events of his past, wondering why such tragedy had befallen him. He would spend hours lost in thought, questioning the meaning of it all, but never finding any solace. In fact, he began to push away any positive emotions that managed to creep into his life, deeming them a luxury he couldn't afford. After all, what was the point of feeling happy when the world was such a treacherous place? At work, Henry became notorious for being constantly watchful, eyeing customers with suspicion as they approached the checkout line. His coworkers began to notice that he would often nod off during breaks, only to jolt awake at the slightest sound. Even his sleep was fitful, as he lay in bed listening for any sign of intruders. When memories of the war did surface, Henry felt numb and disconnected, as if they belonged to someone else. Yet, when he closed his eyes, vivid images would flash before him: the burning buildings, the screams of the wounded, the faces of the dead. These visual memories haunted him, refusing to be silenced. Sometimes, when a car backfired or a plane flew low overhead, Henry felt like he was right back in the midst of battle. The past and present blurred together, leaving him breathless and disoriented. As time went on, Henry began to withdraw from social interactions, afraid that others might pose a threat. He stopped attending church, citing a loss of faith in a higher power that could allow such atrocities to occur. Even his work at the grocery store became increasingly isolating, as he grew convinced that customers and coworkers alike were plotting against him. Despite these efforts to shield himself from harm, Henry couldn't shake the feeling that he was no longer capable of navigating the world. Simple tasks like grocery shopping or paying bills left him feeling anxious and overwhelmed. In recent weeks, Henry's anxiety has become unbearable. His boss at the grocery store called him into her office, concerned about his increasingly erratic behavior. For the first time in years, Henry felt compelled to seek help, though he fears that even therapy might not be enough to quiet the demons of his past. As he sits in the therapist's waiting room, fidgeting with his hat and eyeing the other patients warily, Henry can't help but wonder if anyone will ever truly understand what it means to live in a world where danger lurks around every corner.
